newsitem.title: UK: USSR planned own Star Wars' defences - Jane's.
newsitem.headline: USSR planned own Star Wars' defences - Jane's.

text.p: The former Soviet Union tried to develop a satellite defence network in the 1980s at the same time it was attacking U.S. plans to build a "Star Wars" system, the Jane's defence analysis group said on Friday.

An article in the May edition of the Jane's Intelligence Review said Soviet specialists had worked on a series of complex space battle stations to repel U.S. missile attacks as well as destroying enemy satellites and space shuttles.

The planned network was more complex than the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) -- designed to destroy Soviet ballistic missiles in space -- which was backed by U.S. President Ronald Reagan in the early 1980s, Jane's said.

Author Steven Zaloga said Soviet scientists had been toying with the idea of space-based weaponry as early as the 1960s and in 1976 began work on a programme to develop new ballistic missiles and space platforms to fire them from.

One firm was told to devise a system which could destroy at least 99.8 percent of 10,000 incoming warheads and cruise missiles in five to 25 minutes. Perhaps not surprisingly, the firm concluded this was not practical.

"In spite of the lack of satisfactory progress on many of these exotic techniques, the programme took on new importance in the early 1980s when...Reagan announced the initiation of the SDI," Zaloga wrote.

Parts of the Soviet general staff were convinced Washington wanted to deploy a comprehensive array of 'space strike systems' capable not only of shooting down missiles but also of attacking Soviet objectives on land, sea and air.

"In parallel to this acceleration of the space strike programme, in August 1983 (then Soviet leader Yuri) Andropov initiated a diplomatic offensive to reach an agreement with the U.S. to ban tests and deployment of any type of space-based weapons," he wrote.
"The Soviet Union also announced a unilateral moratorium on orbiting any type of anti-satellite interceptor, even though (their) efforts were funding precisely such programmes."

The Soviet plan was to deploy a mixed force of battle stations, with missile-armed variants deployed to attack satellites in low-earth orbit while laser battle stations engaged targets in high orbits.
The most elaborate project was a massive battle station playing host to four or more combat modules armed with ballistic missiles and unpowered nuclear glide bombs.
"This system, which violated prevailing treaties on the militarisation of space, apparently did not proceed beyond design studies," Zaloga wrote.
The Soviet programme ran into trouble in 1987 when a testbed laser system sent up into space failed to reach orbit.
The two superpowers gradually lost interest in satellite defences as the Cold War thawed and Moscow's programme lost most of its funding after the Soviet Union collapsed in late 1991.
